As in, is it easier to "just say no" if you've already seen someone OD, or had an alcoholic parent who was abusive to you and/or the other parent during your formative childhood years? I wonder if anti-drug campaigns fail because people need to "see to believe," as in, they don't learn from abstract concepts, scientific evidence, hypothetical scenarios, or even other people's experiences; they have to go ahead and see for themselves how bad something is (or isn't) -- hands-on consequences.

In other words, is anti-drug propaganda defective by design because it only works when you're preaching to the choir? If so, is this just human nature? I can speak from personal experience, my father was a violent alcoholic (and even still, sometimes what you'd call a "dry drunk") who was awful to my mother and me. So was his family, as in, my aunts and uncles and even grandparents. The whole family "chain drank" (poured another glass or opened another can before the first was finished); some of them abused drugs and died young. As a result, I don't even so much as drink coffee, never mind booze. Never smoked anything other than a brisket at a neighbor's Memorial Day barbecue, and the only bad acid I've ever "tripped" on is stomach acid from too much Mexican food on Cinco de Mayo.

I wonder how effective the overdose crisis will be on the so-called drug war, as well how it will be affected by people's interests in "better health" of whatever fashion, where Americans are eschewing soda and Pepsi is losing money, or they're doing the gluten-free thing, wearing Fitbits, quitting smoking, etc. Are people going to be more resistant to trying pot even despite the legalization campaigns, because we all know somebody who died or really screwed up their lives with drugs? Or are they going to separate "corporate" drugs from "natural" ones, and be more accepting of pot than "pharma"?
Is anti-drug propaganda (or any other vice) more convincing to people who've experienced drug casualties in some way, rather than people who haven't tried it or lost anybody yet?

I would guess that someone who's had some negative drug-related experiences would have their overall outlook changed for the worse as far as drugs in general goes. They might not just judge drugs harshly in terms of their own experience, but also judge stuff outside their experience base even if it only partly resembles their experience.

Anti-drug ads don't work because they're based on the false premise that drug addicts don't know that the drugs are bad for them. Scientists have figured out that most drug addicts are completely aware of the fact that their behavior is unhealthy. The truth is that for a variety of reasons, substance abusers get into drugs and start using them so much that it fucks with their neuroplasticity. They end up erasing the neural pathways in their brains that make healthy decisions and replacing them with ones that reinforce their "need" for drugs - even though every logical impulse tells them it's bad for them.

Drug addicts need intensive therapy in order to retrain their brains to reward healthy choices, not bad habits. They don't need sappy sob-story ads to tell them what they already know, and neither does the rest of society.
